name: Lena Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive up to Top Moor Farm for seven, it's beef cattle and about four hundred ewes on the hill, plus hay and silage in summer. Mornings I'm feeding the cattle in the sheds and checking the ewes with the quad bike, afternoons it's fencing, dagging, carrying bales, whatever Mrs Pryce or her nephew Owen needs. I worked in the hotel laundry in town for twenty years until it shut, so I'm three years into this and still learning which end of a ewe is which, as Owen likes to say.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy lambing, honestly, the first live twins I delivered on my own I nearly cried. What's hard is the cold and the pay, I'm on the lowest rate, and we've got barely a month's money saved. Imran's a mechanic at the garage on Station Road, so we get by, but there's no slack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get oversold. At the farm I'd mention it to Owen, he's the one who reads about technology. I'd maybe put a thumbs up on a post about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, and nothing isn't perfect. Mrs Pryce (her boss) is 74, and when she stops, her nephew decides whether Top Moor keeps a hired hand or sells the sheep. With hardly anything saved, that's the worry I already carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Top Moor and try to get my sheep dipping and tractor certificates, so I'm useful whoever runs the place. I'd put twenty-five a week into a savings pot, which Imran and I talked about last year and never did. And I'd ask Owen directly what his plans are, rather than guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little unsettled, mostly about Mrs Pryce, not about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked Owen already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the new one and it feels like it isn't my place. But you're right, I should. If he's going to sell the sheep in three years, I'd rather know now than at Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would twenty-five a week mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no meals out, the cheaper supermarket brands, and Imran giving up the second car he's been doing up in the yard. In a year that's about thirteen hundred, which is a boiler or two months of rent. That's real safety for us.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because these things always get oversold.
I'd mention it to Owen, who **reads about** technology, and leave it there.
think: When Mrs Pryce stops at 74, her nephew decides whether a **hired hand** stays.
With barely **a month** saved, that's the worry I already carry.
do: Get my **sheep dipping** and tractor certificates to stay useful to any owner.
Put **twenty-five a week** into a savings pot, about thirteen hundred a year.
Ask Owen **directly** about his plans for the farm.
feel: A little **unsettled**, mostly about Mrs Pryce's **retirement**, not computers.
S0.quote: Mrs Pryce (her boss) is 74, and when she stops, her nephew decides whether Top Moor keeps a hired hand or sells the sheep.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **succession**: the owner's age, not AI, decides her future.
She has avoided asking about plans because she feels it's **not her place**.
Savings would come from small cuts and Imran giving up his **project car**.

steps.text: Get sheep dipping and tractor certificates this year
Save twenty-five a week, about thirteen hundred a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, let the computers do the forms and the ordering. On a hill farm the paperwork is endless, cattle passports, sheep movement forms. I'd tell my friends from the laundry days that people in offices have it harder now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly good for us. A computer that does the movement forms would save Mrs Pryce (her boss) two evenings a month, and it wouldn't put a single ewe through the race for me. Robots on a hill farm would come slowly, it's rough ground and the weather's mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever app Owen brings in for weighing lambs and recording medicines, because I can see that coming. I'd keep doing the same hands-on work and keep the savings pot going. I wouldn't rush anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit curious, and a bit worried for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bilal does IT support for the council, resetting passwords and fixing laptops. That's exactly answering customers and checking things, isn't it. I'd tell him to start looking around now, before the council decides for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots would come slowly to Top Moor. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I'm guessing. But the quad bike gets stuck twice a winter, and the sheep go where they like. I'd want to see a robot gather four hundred ewes off that hill in the fog before I believed it.

say: I'd call it **sensible** to let computers handle the forms and ordering.
I'd tell friends from the **laundry** days that office workers have it harder now.
think: Software doing **movement forms** saves Mrs Pryce time but won't touch my hands-on work.
Robots on a **hill farm** would come slowly because of rough ground and weather.
do: Learn Owen's **lamb-weighing** and medicine app when he brings it in.
Keep the same hands-on work and the **savings pot** going.
feel: Mostly **fine** and curious, with some **worry** for my son.
S1.quote: A computer that does the movement forms would save Mrs Pryce (her boss) two evenings a month, and it wouldn't put a single ewe through the race for me.
fieldNote: She clearly separates the farm's **paperwork** from her own **hands-on** work.
Her son's **IT support** job is where she sees the real exposure in her family.
She admits she is **guessing** about robots on the hill, which is honest.

steps.text: Learn Owen's app for weighing lambs and recording medicines
Keep feeding cattle and checking ewes as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is serious, and the government needs to tell people like me what the plan is. At the farm I'd ask Owen and Mrs Pryce whether they'd keep me past 2031. I'd read up on it properly instead of scrolling past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, My husband Imran fixes cars and I feed sheep, and in this picture both of us are about three years from being told we're not needed. The thinking AI in 2028 hits Mrs Pryce's paperwork and Imran's diagnostics, and then the robots follow us both into the shed and the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to look for work that needs a person in the room, maybe at the auction mart or helping at the vet practice in town, both need people with stock experience. I'd double the savings to fifty a week, even if it hurts. And I'd use the phone assistant more, to help me write job applications, which I'm bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly worried. But I like having a list, it calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the auction mart or the vets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the mart is noise and people and animals all at once, and buyers like to see a face when they're bidding. At the vets, frightened farmers need someone to talk to while the vet is busy. Machines would come there last, I think, though I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Imran say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table and Imran would say his garage boss will buy the robot the day it's cheaper than him, and he'd be right. Then we'd write down everything we pay for and cross things off. We've done that before, when the laundry closed.

say: I'd call this one **serious** and ask the government for a **plan**.
I'd ask Owen and Mrs Pryce whether they'd keep me past **2031**.
think: Imran and I are both about **three years** from not being needed.
Thinking AI hits **paperwork and diagnostics** first, then robots follow into the shed and garage.
do: Look for work at the **auction mart** or **vet practice** that needs a person.
Double the savings to **fifty a week**, even if it hurts.
Use the phone assistant to write **job applications**.
feel: **Properly worried**, though having a **list** calms me down.
S2.quote: My husband Imran fixes cars and I feed sheep, and in this picture both of us are about three years from being told we're not needed.
fieldNote: She thinks about **both earners**, since her husband's garage work faces the same timeline.
The **three-year** gap is time to move toward people-facing jobs, not to learn robots.
She stays steady by **making lists**, as she did when the laundry closed.

steps.text: Apply for work at the auction mart or the vet practice
Double household savings to fifty a week
Use the phone assistant to write job applications

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time, so let's not do anything daft. At the farm I'd talk to Owen about how long he plans to keep the sheep. I'd tell my friends to watch what the big farms do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'd be 66, so I'm close to finishing anyway. The worry is Imran, who's two years younger and might lose the garage work earlier. If he goes before me, we're on my bottom-rate wage alone, and that doesn't cover the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Top Moor and keep the savings up at twenty-five a week. Five years is enough to see which farms buy robots first, and I'd rather watch for two years than jump on day one. If Owen buys a robot, I'd ask to learn to run it, because by then someone else will have shown it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. There's time to watch and pick my moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch for two years. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But when the laundry got its big new machines, the ones who rushed to learn them got moved to nights, and the ones who waited got the day shifts on the new kit. I know that's not quite the same thing. I just like to see something work before I bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Imran lost the garage job first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Pryce for more hours, lambing and harvest, and Imran could do private repairs in the yard. Bilal's offered before to help us out, but I'd rather not. We'd manage for a while.

say: I'd say five years gives us **time**, so nobody should do **anything daft**.
I'd tell friends to watch what the **big farms** do first.
think: Robots in **2034** come when I'm 66, close to finishing anyway.
If Imran's **garage job** goes first, my wage alone won't cover the **rent**.
do: Keep working at Top Moor and saving **twenty-five a week**.
Watch for two years, then ask to **run the robot** once it's proven.
feel: **Uneasy** but steadier, with time to **pick my moment**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to see which farms buy robots first, and I'd rather watch for two years than jump on day one.
fieldNote: She waits for **proof** before acting, drawing on her laundry experience.
The real risk here is her **husband's job**, which could go before hers.
She would rather not lean on **her son**, though he has offered.

steps.text: Keep working at Top Moor through to 66
Watch the big farms for two years before learning robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most of us my age will be retired. At the farm, Owen would get excited and I'd let him. I'd tell my friends this is one for the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm 71, so not my problem at work. What stays is the old stuff: Mrs Pryce retiring, Owen deciding about the sheep, and barely a month saved. Imran would have time to adjust before the robots reach garages too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep the savings pot. I'd tell my son Bilal to stop fixing laptops and learn something a person has to do in the room. I'd offer to help him with the course fees if we can find the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the robots, still a little tense about the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find the money for Bilal's course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a few hundred over a year, out of the savings pot, which would hurt. But it's an investment, and he'd pay it back when he's settled. That's how my father did it for me with my driving lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Bilal learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe physiotherapy, or plumbing like his cousin. Something where a person has to be in the room. I'd leave it to him, but I'd push a bit.

say: I'd say ten years is long, and most people **my age** will be retired.
I'd tell friends this picture is one for the **grandchildren**.
think: Robots in **2039** come at 71, after I've stopped working.
The old worries stay: Mrs Pryce **retiring** and barely a month saved.
do: Keep working at Top Moor and keep the **savings pot** going.
Push Bilal to learn a trade where a person is **in the room**.
Help with his **course fees**, a few hundred over a year.
feel: Fairly **calm** about robots, a little **tense** about the farm's future.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Bilal to stop fixing laptops and learn something a person has to do in the room.
fieldNote: With a decade, the robots pass her by, but **farm succession** still keeps her uneasy.

steps.text: Keep working at Top Moor and saving weekly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Imran and I would both be hit within about three years and we've got nothing behind us. What would help is plain warning from employers, so you know a year ahead, and help finding work with animals and people, like the mart.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age get told last. I'm not against the machines, I'm against finding out last. Give me a year's notice and I'll sort myself out.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machines, I'm against finding out last.
portrait: Lena is 58, a former **hotel laundry** worker three years into work on a hill beef and sheep farm.
She and her husband Imran, a **mechanic**, have barely a month saved and no slack.
She uses AI **now and then** and waits for proof before changing, as she learned at the laundry.
Her biggest pressure is **farm succession**, since the owner is 74 and the nephew may sell the sheep.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** because both earners face it, while slower pictures leave her uneasy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Imran would both lose work within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Plain **warning** from employers, ideally a year ahead.
Help finding work with **animals and people**, such as the auction mart.
